# Times Now

> Times Now is a digital news publisher covering breaking news, India news, world news, politics, business, technology, sports, entertainment, lifestyle, and major national and international events.

## Official Website

- [Times Now](https://www.timesnownews.com/): Times Now delivers the latest news and editorial coverage across India and the world, including breaking news, politics, business, technology, sports, entertainment, education, and lifestyle. Stay updated with real-time news and major developments shaping India and the world.

## Times Now Main Categories

- India News: https://www.timesnownews.com/india (Latest national news, state updates, politics, government decisions, and public affairs.)
- World News: https://www.timesnownews.com/world (Global events, international relations, and geopolitical developments.)
- Entertainment News: https://www.timesnownews.com/entertainment-news (Latest movie releases, celebrity news, reviews, and box office updates.)
- Lifestyle: https://www.timesnownews.com/lifestyle (Health, wellness, travel, food, culture, and everyday lifestyle trends.)
- Cities News: https://www.timesnownews.com/city (Local news, city updates, civic issues, traffic and important developments.)
- Auto News: https://www.timesnownews.com/auto (Latest car and bike launches, reviews, prices, EVs, and automobile industry updates.)
- Spiritual: https://www.timesnownews.com/spiritual (Religious news, festivals, temple updates, spiritual teachings, and traditions.)
- Astrology: https://www.timesnownews.com/astrology (Daily horoscopes, zodiac predictions, kundli, and planetary update.)
- Business News: https://www.timesnownews.com/business-economy (Business developments, economy, corporate news, companies, and financial updates.)
- Technology & Science: https://www.timesnownews.com/technology-science (Latest tech news, gadgets, smartphones, AI innovations.)
- Education: https://www.timesnownews.com/education (Board exam updates, results, entrance exams, admissions, and education news.)
- Sports: https://www.timesnownews.com/sports (Cricket, football, and other sports news, including live scores, schedules, results, and analysis.)
- Videos: https://www.timesnownews.com/videos (Latest news videos, interviews, live coverage, viral videos from India and around the world)

## Breaking News & Latest News Coverage
 
- Times Now LIVE TV: https://www.timesnownews.com/live-tv
- Latest News: https://www.timesnownews.com/latest-news

## Tools & Utilities
Weather: https://www.timesnownews.com/weather (Check Today's Weather Forecast and AQI in Your City.)
Gold Rates: https://www.timesnownews.com/gold-rates (Latest gold prices and daily rate updates across India)
Silver Rates: https://www.timesnownews.com/silver-rates (Latest silver prices and daily rate updates across India.)

## Times Now Content publishes:

- Breaking news and developing stories.
- Live blogs and real-time event updates.
- News explainers and opinion.
- Interviews and analysis.
- Product, technology, and entertainment reviews.
- Elections, major events, schedules, and results coverage.
- Photo Galleries
- Special Reports
- Movie Reviews

## Editorial Standards

- Prioritize factual accuracy, clarity, relevance, and original reporting.
- Attribute statements, quotations, and claims to their sources wherever appropriate.
- Distinguish confirmed facts from allegations, forecasts, opinions, and unverified claims.
- Preserve the context of reports, especially for developing stories and live blogs.


## Content Discovery

- Website: https://www.timesnownews.com/
- Google News Sitemap: https://www.timesnownews.com/google-news-sitemap-en.xml
- RSS Feed: https://www.timesnownews.com/info/rssfeed
- Author profiles: https://www.timesnownews.com/author

## Trust & Editorial

- About Us: https://www.timesnownews.com/info/about-us 
- Contact Us: https://www.timesnownews.com/info/contact-us
- Privacy Policy: https://www.timesnownews.com/info/privacy-policy
- Disclaimer: https://www.timesnownews.com/info/disclaimer
- Complaint Redressal: https://www.timesnownews.com/info/complaint-redressal
- Terms of use: https://www.timesnownews.com/info/terms-conditions

Instead, the ritual was conducted at the usual spot, citing law and order concerns. Rahul Gandhi, who has previously identified himself as a \"true Hindu,\" has been criticized for not addressing the controversy. The temple board, which is under the state government’s control, has been blamed for not authorizing the lighting of the Deepam as per the court's directive.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\n\u003ch2\u003eBroader Implications and Historical Context\u003c/h2\u003e\nThe incident has also brought attention to the broader issue of how Hindu rituals and temples are managed in Tamil Nadu. Meanwhile, Congress leaders have downplayed the public disagreements, describing them as routine negotiation tactics. Political analysts suggest that the SP's firm stance may stem from lessons learned in previous alliances, such as the one with the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) in Bihar, where the Congress's performance fell short of expectations.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\nAs the negotiations continue, it remains uncertain whether the two parties can resolve their differences and present a united front against the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. After airstrikes nearby, photographs showed windows blown out, floors covered in debris and the hall's decorative mosaics shattered by the blast. According to UNESCO, \"the Golestan Palace in Tehran, a UNESCO World Heritage site, was reportedly damaged by debris and the shock wave following an airstrike to the Arag Square, located in the buffer zone of the site in the Iranian capital.\"\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eIt wasn't the only heritage casualty of war. The year began with an attack on Kyiv's Pechersk Lavra in January, its first wartime damage since the Second World War. By the end of February, war had reached Iran, and within two weeks shockwaves had broken the mirrors of Golestan and damaged Chehel Sotoun in Isfahan. In March, a strike hit the entrance of the Al-Bass archaeological site in Tyre. In June, a drone strike set the roof of the Lavra's Dormition Cathedral on fire, and in July UNESCO put Tyre on its list of World Heritage in Danger. On 20 November, with the year almost over, attacks damaged St Volodymyr's Cathedral in Kyiv and 12 heritage sites in Odesa. Three countries, eleven months, and places meant to be protected were hit again and again. And these are just a few examples of the damage.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Debris lies inside Golestan Palace following airstrikes. (Photo: Reuters/File)\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156574853\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"167121\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Debris lies inside Golestan Palace following airstrikes. (Photo: Reuters/File)\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThe US and Israel's war on Iran began on 28 February. Golestan is a 400-year-old complex of eight main palace structures and one of the best examples of Qajar-era architecture. It became a collateral damage of the war. In Isfahan, a strike on 10 March near government offices damaged the 17th-century Chehel Sotoun Palace, part of the UNESCO-listed Persian Garden property. Officials said the damage worsened in the weeks after the blasts. The Masjed-e Jame mosque and buildings near the prehistoric caves of the Khorramabad Valley were also affected. Iran's heritage ministry reported that around 149 historical monuments across 18 provinces and 29 cities had been damaged in the war. Conservators have collected broken decorative fragments and made emergency repairs. Mirror work and painted ceilings can be remade, though the original material cannot be brought back.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eLebanon suffered massively as the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah escalated. The first strike on 6 March, hit the entrance of Tyre's Al-Bass archaeological site, and Lebanon's culture ministry reported material damage to the entrance. Tyre was once a major Phoenician port, and Al-Bass holds a necropolis some three thousand years old, next to a Roman hippodrome and triumphal arch. On 7 June, according to International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS), strikes damaged the entrance precinct, administration buildings and archaeological warehouses. Experts could not assess the ruins because of the security situation. ICOMOS Lebanon described the cultural loss as irreversible. On 13 April, a strike damaged the shrine of the Prophet Shamoun al-Safa beside the crusader-built Shamaa Castle. In July, UNESCO put the historical city of Tyre on its List of World Heritage in Danger.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"The Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra burns after it was hit during Russian missile and drone strikes in Kyiv, Ukraine, June 15. (Photo: Reuters/File)\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156574862\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"79105\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;The Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra burns after it was hit during Russian missile and drone strikes in Kyiv, Ukraine, June 15. (Photo: Reuters/File)\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eUkraine's war began in 2022, and the heritage toll builds year on year. What happened in 2026 includes the first wartime damage to the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra since the Second World War, on 24 January. On 15 June, a larger strike hit the Lavra's Dormition Cathedral, and fire burned around 800 square metres of roofing before firefighters stopped it reaching the wooden iconostasis. Russia denied striking the monastery and blamed a US-made Patriot missile. On 20 November, attacks damaged St Volodymyr's Cathedral in Kyiv and 12 heritage sites in Odesa, whose historic centre is on UNESCO's danger list. As of that date, UNESCO had verified damage to 573 cultural sites since the full-scale invasion began. That includes 165 religious sites, 294 historic or artistic buildings, 44 museums, 33 monuments, 24 libraries, eight archaeological sites and five archives. Ukraine's culture ministry counts 2,185 damaged heritage sites by the end of October, 48 of them completely destroyed, and 2,686 damaged cultural institutions, again since 2022. Roofs and masonry can be rebuilt. Frescoes and wooden interiors are harder to save. The Dormition Cathedral itself was destroyed in 1941 and rebuilt in the late 20th century, so it now carries a second wound.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Sudan\u0026amp;#39;s ancient pyramids of Meroë face growing threats from the ongoing civil war and deteriorating conservation conditions. (Photo: iStock)\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156574886\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"98989\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Sudan\u0026amp;#39;s ancient pyramids of Meroë face growing threats from the ongoing civil war and deteriorating conservation conditions. (Photo: iStock)\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eElsewhere, the record also spans years. UNESCO's assessment for Gaza, updated in March, recorded damage to 164 cultural sites since October 2023. In Sudan, it reported in April that more than 100 cultural sites had been damaged and at least 22 museums looted or destroyed since the war began. It was reported by UNESCO  in April, as the war in Sudan entered its fourth year, that more than 100 cultural sites had been damaged and at least 22 museums looted or destroyed since April 2023. The looting of the National Museum in Khartoum took place earlier in the war, and one storage annex there held more than 10,000 objects from the international campaign to save Nubian heritage in the 1960s. In August, \u003cem\u003eAP\u003c/em\u003e reported that the fighting threatened the Meroe pyramids, with preservation work halted.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eHistoric sites hold the memory of communities and carry artistic and architectural traditions across generations. The 1954 Hague Convention requires parties to respect cultural property and take steps to protect it during wars and armed conflicts. The violence unleashed this year has cost human lives, and it has also taken heritage and culture, much of which can never be rebuilt. Under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, intentionally directing attacks against cultural property that is not a military objective may constitute a war crime. Beyond these alleged financial demands, some parents have had to look beyond their preferred schools, accept longer commutes and make difficult compromises to secure a seat. These experiences raise a larger question: what does it really take to get a child into a school of choice?\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThese experiences persist despite clear rules prohibiting schools from seeking such 'favours'. In its November 20 circular for the 2027–28 admission cycle, the \u003ca href=\"https://www.timesnownews.com/education/nursery-admissions-2027-delhi-schools-reveal-point-system-check-if-your-child-qualifies-article-156559771\" data-type=\"tilCustomLink\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eDirectorate of Education (DoE)\u003c/a\u003e reiterated that schools cannot collect capitation fees or donations from parents at the time of admission. The circular defines capitation fee as any donation, contribution or payment over and above the fee notified by the school. Violations can attract a fine of up to ten times the amount collected.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eBut let's see how the admission process plays out for parents on the ground. Times Now Digital spoke to several parents to understand their experiences, the additional demands they encountered and the compromises they made while trying to secure a school seat for their children.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhen Nursery Admissions Start Feeling Like A Competition\u003cbr /\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eFor the mother of three-year-old Mishi, the search began with some of Delhi's reputed schools. But navigating different points-based criteria, distance requirements and the possibility of a draw of lots soon made the process complicated. The family also heard about hefty donations being sought at one or two schools.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e“The more we explored the admission process, the more complicated it seemed. What was concerning was hearing about hefty donations or additional payments at some schools. It made us wonder whether meeting the official criteria was enough or whether families also needed to be prepared to spend significantly more,” the parent said.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThe family eventually looked at schools in Noida, but some of the institutions they preferred had high fee structures too. They finally chose a school after weighing the quality of education, affordability and convenience.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e“As parents, you want the best for your child, but the pressure to get into a reputed school sometimes makes you lose sight of what matters most. At just three years of age, a child shouldn't become the centre of such intense competition,” the parent added.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eFor Ankit, who lives in Shreshtha Vihar, the search eventually narrowed down to three schools. “The admission process was far more difficult than we had anticipated. With the points system and the lottery determining admissions in certain situations, our options became increasingly limited,” he said. Of the three schools the family seriously considered, two expected additional payments in the name of donations. The family eventually chose Ahlcon Public School in Mayur Vihar, where no such payment was sought.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eBut the choice came with a nearly two-hour daily commute. His six-year-old daughter takes almost an hour each way to reach school and often returns home tired.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e“We wanted the best for our daughter, but in the process, we have had to make compromises that affect her everyday routine. The commute takes away from the time she could otherwise spend playing, resting or pursuing other activities,” Ankit said.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e“It makes us question whether getting into a reputed school should come at such a cost. A good school should give a child opportunities to grow, but the journey to get there shouldn't leave them exhausted,” he added.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAn IIT-Level Race For A Nursery Seat?\u003cbr /\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eFor Mohit, an \u003ca href=\"https://www.timesnownews.com/education/iit-delhi-leads-india-in-global-sustainability-rankings-secures-194th-spot-worldwide-article-156522069\" data-type=\"tilCustomLink\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eIIT Delhi\u003c/a\u003e graduate and software engineer, the nursery admission process has brought an unexpected comparison with competitive examinations. His wife is a Chartered Accountant, and the couple is exploring schools in Delhi and Gurugram for their son.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e“I didn't know my son would have to go through the same tough competition that I did to get into an IIT. The only difference is, he has to get into nursery school, which is absolutely bizarre for me,” he said.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eMohit has heard of instances where families were asked to make donations or pay additional amounts, although he has not personally faced such a demand. He is also apprehensive that parents' professional backgrounds and perceived financial standing could influence expectations around payments.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e“I sometimes wonder whether having well-paying jobs could actually work against us by making schools expect us to pay more,” he said.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eDelhi's admission guidelines prohibit schools from using parents' educational qualifications as a selection criterion. Yet, concerns about how parents' professional identities may figure in admission decisions are not entirely absent.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eAn earlier admission experience at a sought-after Noida school offers another example. A journalist seeking nursery admission for her child was called, along with her husband, for a parent interaction. The school later offered their child a seat. Her work as an education journalist was taken into account during the process, raising questions about the factors that may influence a school's admission decision beyond its published criteria.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eAn unexpected admission expense can also take a significant bite out of a family's savings, says Rahul Banerjee, Founder and Managing Director of PGP Academy and Founder of PGP Wealth. He points out that such a payment can force parents to dip into money set aside for emergencies, particularly if they have not planned for admission-related costs. “An unexpected admission expense of ₹2 lakh could consume nearly 33% of a family's ₹6 lakh financial safety net, assuming a monthly income of ₹1.5 lakh. Parents should plan ahead, ask for itemised fee schedules and question unauthorised donations. December 1778, Philip Francis, a member of the governor-general's council in Calcutta, climbed a bamboo ladder into the bedroom of a young married woman and was caught there. Her husband sued and won 50,000 sicca rupees. Two years later a weekly paper printed the case all over again, this time with a dissenting judge's doubts about the evidence. The paper was Hicky's Bengal Gazette, India's first newspaper, and its surviving pages, scattered for nearly two and a half centuries, can now be read online.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThe American historian Andrew Otis, who holds a PhD in journalism, has launched hickysgazette.com, a searchable archive that puts every known surviving issue in chronological order alongside transcriptions. Anyone who enjoys history through its gossip and its grudges will lose an evening to it.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eA Paper That Lasted Two Years\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eJames Augustus Hicky, an Irishman, printed the first issue on 29 January 1780. It came out every Saturday under the motto \"Open to all parties, but influenced by none\", and the last issue appeared on 30 March 1782. In those two years Hicky produced 121 issues and a prospectus, 464 pages in all.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"James Augustus Hicky Challenged the British with India\u0026amp;#39;s First Newspaper\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156569089\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"187082\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;James Augustus Hicky Challenged the British with India\u0026amp;#39;s First Newspaper\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eNo institution holds a complete set. Otis found seven incomplete collections in six archives across India, the United Kingdom, Germany, Australia and the United States. He fitted them together into the fullest run of the paper assembled since Hicky stopped printing.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eHe started during a Fulbright fellowship in Kolkata. The National Library of India had copies but would not let him photograph or scan them, so he bought paper photocopies, took them home and scanned them himself. His best find came later, in the record room of the Calcutta High Court, where a special edition dated 25 June 1781 had lain for more than 230 years. In it Hicky argued for the freedom of the press, after the governor-general's council had moved against his paper.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eMocking the Mighty\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eHicky kept clear of politics at first. Within months he was going after the most powerful men in Bengal, usually by nickname, which made him harder to sue and more fun to read.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThe chief justice, Elijah Impey, was \"Poolbundy\", a reference to allegations about contracts for repairing Bengal's embankments. Justice Robert Chambers became \"Sir Viner Pliant\", a jab at his academic background and his alleged closeness to the governor-general, Warren Hastings, whom Hicky called a tyrant. He accused the Swedish missionary Johann Zachariah Kiernander of misusing money meant for educating orphans. He even used the classified columns. One mock notice reported that sincerity and honesty had gone missing, and another advertised for someone who would neither offer nor accept bribes.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eSome of the jokes need footnotes now. The complaints behind them, about officials who seemed to be enriching themselves, need none.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eThe Francis Affair\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eFrancis was Hastings's bitter rival on the council. The woman on the other side of the window was Catherine Grand, wife of the East India Company official George Francis Grand. When Hicky returned to the case in his edition of 24 February 1781 and printed the dissenting judge's opinion, he was reopening a verdict the city's establishment wanted left alone. Catherine Grand later married Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, Napoleon's foreign minister, so the woman at the centre of a Calcutta bedroom scandal ended up at the French court.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Catherine Grand, at the Centre of a 1778 Calcutta Scandal that Hicky Revived in 1781.\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156568984\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"1145812\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Catherine Grand, at the Centre of a 1778 Calcutta Scandal that Hicky Revived in 1781 (Picture Credit - Wikipedia)\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eWhat the Advertisements Show\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThe advertisements may end up being the archive's most useful pages, because they record the city's ordinary business in its own words.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eA notice dated 19 February 1780 offered a property with fruit trees for sale, together with two enslaved Africans, as part of the estate of the late Andrew Stein. They appear in the same columns as houses and furniture, which is exactly what makes the notice so disturbing to read today.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Calcutta in the Late 18th Century\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156569039\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"3276202\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Calcutta in the Late 18th Century \u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eElsewhere there is a garden and bungalow near China Bazaar, and an auction of a wet dock, warehouses and vessels near the Old Fort. Another notice shows that Calcutta had a commercial circulating library well before many of its better-known educational and cultural institutions. That last detail will interest anyone tracing how people in the city got hold of books in the 1780s.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eCensorship, Prison and Closure\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThe authorities moved against Hicky quickly. A notice of 14 November 1780 recorded an official order barring the paper from the postal system. It was a way of hurting a newspaper without banning it, by cutting off its readers. Libel proceedings followed, and in June 1781 Hicky went to prison. He kept the paper going from jail for several months. In March 1782, the authorities seized his press and his type, and the Gazette closed.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Old Government House, Calcutta\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156569081\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"3614636\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Old Government House, Calcutta\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eIndian journalism has argued with power many times since. Its first printer went to prison after libel proceedings over his attacks on the most powerful men in Bengal, and he kept publishing from his cell.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eThe Book Behind the Archive\u003cbr /\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eOtis first set out this history in his book 'Hicky's Bengal Gazette: The Untold Story of India's First Newspaper', published in 2018, which follows Hicky's career and the colonial city he infuriated. The archive gives readers the sources behind it. You can read a chapter, then open the original pages it draws on and judge Otis's reading for yourself.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Hicky\u0026amp;#39;s Bengal Gazette: The Untold Story of India\u0026amp;#39;s First Newspaper\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156569083\" hostid=\"183\" sizebytes=\"130928\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Hicky\u0026amp;#39;s Bengal Gazette: The Untold Story of India\u0026amp;#39;s First Newspaper (Picture Credit - Penguin)\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eBecause the transcriptions are searchable, a single name can be followed from issue to issue, which no reader of the scattered originals could easily do. For family historians, students of colonial Calcutta and novelists looking for period detail, that is the archive's practical value: the paper can finally be read as Hicky's subscribers read it, one Saturday after another.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eGive hickysgazette.com an evening. Search for a street, a trade or a surname you recognise, and see what Calcutta was selling, renting and gossiping about in 1780. If a page hooks you, pick up Otis's book for the life of the man who printed it, and keep the archive open beside you while you read.\u003cmeta content=\"cms.next\" name=\"cmsei\" /\u003e","cmstype":"ARTICLE","status":"ACTIVE","title":"India's First Newspaper Returns After 246 Years With Stories Of Scandal and Colonial Secret","cmssource":"CMSLITE","parenttitle":"Books","titleforurl":"india's first newspaper returns after 246 years with stories of scandal and colonial secret","synopsis":"A bamboo ladder, a jailed printer, a chief justice nicknamed Poolbundy. Kulthe's shift began at 8 pm. On 26 November 2008, she took charge of the antenatal ward at Cama and Albless Hospital for Women and Children in South Mumbai, where 20 women in the advanced stages of pregnancy were waiting to give birth. She expected a night of blood pressure checks and perhaps a delivery or two. Before it was over, two gunmen had stormed the hospital grounds, and she had hidden all 20 women from them.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eEighteen years on, as Mumbai marks the anniversary of the attacks, Kulthe's account of that night remains one of the clearest pictures of what happened inside the hospital, told by a nurse whose first thought throughout was her patients. She has since repeated it as a witness at Kasab's trial and before the United Nations Security Council.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eWhat Happened At Cama Hospital That Night\u003cbr /\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eCama and Albless is a state-run hospital for women and children, built in the 1880s with money from the Parsi philanthropist Pestonjee Hormusjee Cama. On the night of 26/11, two of the ten Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists who had landed in Mumbai, Ajmal Kasab and Abu Ismail, reached its compound after the shootings at Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e    \u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Cama and Albless is a State-Run Hospital for Women and Children\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156564184\" hostid=\"183\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Cama and Albless is a State-Run Hospital for Women and Children (Picture Credit - Wikipedia)\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eAt around 10.30 pm, Kulthe heard firing behind the building. She went to a window with a colleague and saw two armed men who had climbed over the compound wall. One of them shot at the window, and the bullet missed Kulthe but hit the helper beside her. From the same window, she could see the hospital's security guards lying in a pool of blood near the gate. The gunmen then started up through the building, towards the floor where her ward was.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eHow Did One Nurse Protect 20 Pregnant Women\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eKulthe shut the ward's two thick doors and locked its iron gate. At the far end of the ward was a small pantry, cramped but safer than the open beds, and she moved all 20 women and a few of their relatives into it, whispering that they would be safe there.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eShe switched off the lights and asked everyone to silence their phones. Many of the women were close to their due dates, and keeping them calm in the dark meant talking to them constantly in a low voice. Above them, the gunmen had reached the terrace and were firing at the police below and throwing grenades.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e    \u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Anjali Kulthe, The Nurse Who Protected 20 Pregnant Women During 26/11 Attacks\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156564206\" hostid=\"183\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Anjali Kulthe, The Nurse Who Protected 20 Pregnant Women During 26/11 Attacks\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eKulthe kept working through all of it. She took an injured colleague down to casualty and treated her. When one of the women in the pantry went into labour, Kulthe walked her to the delivery room, where a doctor delivered the baby safely while the staff tried to make no noise. A second woman, whose blood pressure was dangerously high, then went into labour too. The doctor could not come down because of the firing, so Kulthe persuaded the frightened woman to leave the pantry, took her to the staircase and handed her to the staff waiting there.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThen she went back to her ward and sat with the others. By her own account, she kept them hidden for about three hours, until the police knocked on the door in the morning and brought them out. \"At all cost, I wanted to protect my patients,\" she said later.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eThe Price The City Paid Around The Hospital\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eThe attackers had meant to kill patients, and they failed because the staff had locked every ward. The night still took a heavy toll in and around Cama, where around seven people were killed inside the hospital and nine outside it. Among the dead were three of Mumbai's most senior police officers, Anti-Terrorism Squad chief Hemant Karkare, Additional Commissioner Ashok Kamte and Senior Inspector Vijay Salaskar, who were killed trying to stop the two gunmen. Abu Ismail was shot dead later that night near Girgaon Chowpatty. Kasab was captured alive, the only one of the ten attackers to survive.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e    \u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Remembering The Brave Police Officers Who Sacrificed Lives During 26/11\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156564218\" hostid=\"183\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Remembering The Brave Police Officers Who Sacrificed Lives During 26/11\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eWhy Did She Choose To Testify\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eAbout a month after the attacks, Mumbai Police asked Kulthe to identify Kasab. Her family was frightened. \"My family was scared when I was called to identify Kasab in court, but I decided to testify,\" she said. She asked to appear in her nurse's uniform and became a witness at his trial.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eWhen she picked him out in jail, she recalled, Kasab smiled and said, \"Madam, you've identified me. I am Ajmal Kasab.\" Her evidence and that of other witnesses helped convict him in May 2010, and he was executed on 21 November 2012.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e    \u003cdiv type=\"image\" title=\"Ajmal Kasab Was The Only Surviving Terrorist Of Mumbai\u0026amp;#39;s 26:11 Attacks\" primecategoryid=\"400\" msid=\"156564258\" hostid=\"183\" caption=\"\u0026amp;lt;p\u0026amp;gt;Ajmal Kasab Was The Only Surviving Terrorist Of Mumbai\u0026amp;#39;s 26:11 Attacks\u0026amp;lt;/p\u0026amp;gt;\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003eIn December 2022, Kulthe spoke by video link at a United Nations Security Council briefing on counterterrorism. She told the delegates about the 20 women in her care, about the trauma that survivors and victims' families still live with, and about the lack of remorse Kasab showed when she faced him.\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eA Nurse Who Stayed At Her Post\u003cbr /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003c/h2\u003eWhen Kulthe talks about that night, she talks about her patients and what she owed them as their nurse. She had no weapon, only a set of locked doors, a dark pantry and the patience to keep 20 frightened women quiet for hours. The film 'Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata' later drew on her story in its fictionalised portrait of the nurses of Cama Hospital. The antenatal ward at Cama still fills with women waiting to give birth, and the night shift still begins at 8 pm.
